title: The Ethiopian Canon
subtitle: What It Contains and Why It Matters
description:
Open almost any Bible and turn to the table of contents. Sixty-six books. Now open the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church's own list: eighty-one.

What are the extra books? Who decided what counts as Scripture? And why did so few of us ever hear that an African church had been translating, copying, counting and explaining its Bible for more than sixteen centuries?

The Ethiopian Canon is a 395-page, carefully sourced guide for readers who want the real answers. It lays out the Ethiopian church's own list exactly as the Church publishes it, shows how the number 81 is reached in more than one way, and explains why “fifteen extra books” is the wrong way to think about it.

Along the way it follows the story from Aksum and the Ge’ez Scriptures, through the scribes who kept the parchment pages and the teachers who explained them line by line, to the printed Bible — and then crosses the ocean to the Black American tradition that read the word “Ethiopia” in Psalm 68:31 for two centuries before it could read Ethiopia’s books.

Every reading is marked as a reading. Every claim can be checked on the page. No secrets to sell, no symbols to borrow — just a record you can read for yourself.

Inside the book

  • Six parts, 27 chapters — from “The Bible We Inherited” to “The Reader Who Can Pass It On.”
  • The Canon Atlas — the Church’s own list of eighty-one, set beside the other ways the Ethiopian tradition has recorded the number.
  • Book Guide, A to Z — the names you have least likely heard: Tegsats, Ezra Sutuel, Josephas son of Bengorion, Sirate Tsion and more.
  • A Timeline from Aksum to Harlem — the Ethiopian Scriptures beside the English Bible in Black America.
  • The Edition Checklist — five questions to ask of any English book that calls itself an “Ethiopian Bible.”
  • The Foundation Ledger, Glossary, Bibliography and Index — so a reading group can check the argument for itself.

A book you can trust

Scripture quotations are from the King James Version; 1 Enoch is quoted from R. H. Charles (public domain). The Ethiopian church’s list is quoted from its own English-language website. This is an independent work of study, not an official publication of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, and it does not speak for it.

Digital edition (PDF). Instant access from your Account page after purchase. A free Study Circle Guide for groups is available separately on the Free Resources page.

who_for:
• Bible readers who noticed that the table of contents is not the same in every church — and want a clear, calm, honest explanation.
  • Black Christians and readers of African heritage who want to understand Ethiopia’s place in the history of Scripture.
  • Sunday school teachers, pastors and small-group leaders looking for a trustworthy resource (with a free seven-session study guide).
  • Curious readers who have seen viral videos about “the hidden books of the Bible” and want to separate fact from hype.
  • Students and self-learners who like sources, citations and a method they can reuse.

No background in Hebrew, Greek or Ge’ez is needed. No one is asked to give up their own Bible.

faq.question: What format is the book, and how do I get it?
faq.answer: It is a digital PDF edition of 395 pages. After you check out, sign in to your Account page with the email you used to buy and press Download — your purchase is waiting there, and you can download it again any time.

faq.question: Is this an official publication of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church?
faq.answer: No. It is an independent work of study. It quotes the Church's own published list and its own words, but it does not speak for the Church or for any other church body.

faq.question: Do I have to agree that the Ethiopian list is the "right" Bible?
faq.answer: No. The book does not ask you to give up your Bible. A reader with sixty-six books can keep them and still read Enoch with understanding; an Ethiopian Orthodox reader can keep eighty-one and still learn from the reasons others gave for a shorter list. Each reading is marked as a reading so you can decide for yourself.

faq.question: Is there a study guide for groups?
faq.answer: Yes. A free Study Circle Guide turns the book into seven sessions (or thirteen weeks) for Bible studies, Sunday school classes, book clubs and families. Download it from the Free Resources page.

faq.question: Can I read it on my phone or tablet?
faq.answer: Yes. The PDF opens on any phone, tablet, e-reader app or computer, and the page numbers in the index are clickable links.

faq.question: Can I share my copy or print it?
faq.answer: The book is sold for your personal use, and copying or redistributing it requires permission, apart from brief quotations. The free Study Circle Guide, however, may be shared freely for non-commercial study.
